# Why Most New Year's Resolutions Fail

Every year, as December comes to an end, we find ourselves making promises to a future version of ourselves. We'll go to the gym, read more books, spend less time on our phones, eat healthier, or finally learn that skill we've been putting off. For a few days, sometimes even a few weeks, we're genuinely committed. And then, slowly, things go back to normal.

So, why does this happen?

I think the biggest reason most New Year's resolutions fail is that we rely too heavily on motivation.

There's something about the beginning of a new year that makes change feel exciting. A fresh calendar, a clean slate, and the feeling that this time things will be different. Motivation is at an all-time high, and suddenly, waking up at 5 AM or going for a run every morning doesn't seem so difficult.

But motivation is an emotion, and like most emotions, it comes and goes.

Eventually, the excitement wears off. You have a long day, it's raining outside, you don't feel like going to the gym, or you simply have other things on your mind. And that's when the real test begins. Unfortunately, most resolutions aren't built to survive those moments.

We often mistake wanting something badly for being prepared to work towards it consistently. The two are very different.

The problem isn't necessarily that we set ambitious goals. It's that we build our plans around the assumption that we'll feel motivated every single day. We forget that progress is rarely exciting. More often than not, it's repetitive, inconvenient, and sometimes downright boring.

I think the solution is to stop treating resolutions as temporary bursts of enthusiasm and start treating them as habits.

Instead of promising to read 30 books in a year, start by reading five pages every day. Instead of committing to an intense workout routine, start with something you can realistically maintain. Make the barrier to starting as small as possible.

And perhaps most importantly, learn to show up even when you don't feel like it.

Missing a day shouldn't mean abandoning the entire goal. One bad week shouldn't become an excuse to give up for the rest of the year.

Ultimately, I don't think the people who achieve their New Year's resolutions are necessarily more motivated than everyone else. They're simply better at continuing when motivation disappears.

Maybe that's what we should focus on this January: not becoming a completely different person overnight, but becoming someone who keeps showing up, even on ordinary days.

# Why resolutions fail: the date was always the problem

I've made New Year's resolutions. I couldn't tell you what any of them were. None of them failed dramatically. I didn't cave in week three and eat a cake with my hands. I just forgot I'd made them, which is somehow worse. You can't even learn from a goal you can't remember.

I think that's how most resolutions actually go, and I think the date is to blame. Not willpower. Not vagueness. January 1st.

**1. Nothing in your life changed on January 1st**

A real reason to change usually comes from something: a comment from a doctor, a bill, a photo, a week that went badly. Resolutions come from a calendar. The year rolled over, so a goal was supposed to follow. But a goal that arrives on schedule has no event holding it in place. It's a promise made because it was the time for promises, which is exactly why it slides off.

**2. You picked it from the menu**

When the date is the prompt, you reach for the stock answers: eat better, move more, read more. Not because those are your problems, but because they're the kind of thing people resolve. A goal chosen from a list was never personal, and nothing impersonal survives a dull Tuesday.

**3. It's a terrible week to start anything**

You're tired, broke, back at work, and every routine you had got scrambled over the holidays. The one day everyone agrees to begin new habits is also one of the worst days of the year to begin anything.

**4. It's annual, so it just expires**

If you set goals once a year, the one that slips has to wait twelve months. Nobody re-sets a resolution in March. It doesn't fail. It quietly reaches the end of its shelf life.

**What to do instead**

- Start when something happens. Tie the goal to an event in your life, not a number on a calendar.
- Pick the thing that's actually bugging you, even if it's boring and nobody else would resolve it.
- Choose an unremarkable start date: a normal Tuesday in a normal week.
- Write it down somewhere you'll see it. Worst case, next January you'll at least know what you forgot.

The calendar isn't going to change you. It can't even get you to remember what you asked it for.

# January 1 Isn't Going to Change Your Life

Every December, we seem to go through the same ritual. We reflect on everything we didn't do, make a mental list of everything we want to change, and convince ourselves that this time will be different. We'll wake up earlier, exercise regularly, read more books, spend less time on our phones, and somehow become a completely different person by February.

We convince ourselves that the beginning of a new year offers some magical opportunity to reinvent ourselves, when, in reality, we're the same people we were on December 31.

The problem, perhaps, isn't that we lack ambition. It's that we keep waiting for the perfect moment to act on it.

We treat personal growth like an annual event rather than an ongoing process. We make ambitious promises to ourselves when motivation is high, only to abandon them when everyday life inevitably gets in the way. And when we miss a day, skip a workout, or fall back into an old habit, we often consider the entire resolution a failure.

But why should missing a week mean abandoning a year?

Maybe we should stop treating January as an opportunity to become someone new and start treating every ordinary Tuesday as an opportunity to become a little better.

There's no countdown, no grand announcement, and no need to wait for the next chapter of the calendar.

Because ultimately, the calendar doesn't change you. What you do with the days on it does.

## The Problem With January 1st

I've made a few New Year's resolutions. I can't tell you what most of them were. That's not a confession, it's the whole point.

The usual explanation for why resolutions fail is that they're badly built. Too vague, too big, no plan. Set smaller goals, track them, stack them onto habits you already have. All true, probably. But it skips over something stranger: why are we all trying to change on the same day?

Every other decision to change comes from somewhere. You start running because your knees ache going up the stairs. You quit something because you catch your reflection and don't like it. You save money because the account hit a number that scared you. The change has a cause, and the cause arrived first.

New Year's Day reverses that. The date shows up and demands a reason. So you go looking for one, and you find something plausible: read more, drink less, call people back. It sounds like a goal. It's really just an answer to the question "well, what are you going to do?"

Nothing in your life has shifted between December 31st and January 1st. Your schedule is the same. The things that made the old habit easy are all still there. The only thing that's different is the calendar, and the calendar has never once stopped anyone from doing anything.

This is why forgetting them is so easy. There's nothing to remember them by. A change you made because of a real moment has that moment attached to it — you can go back to it when you waver. A change you made because it was January has January attached to it, and by the third week that's gone.

I don't think the fix is better resolutions. I think it's noticing that the ones that stick tend to start on unremarkable days, for reasons you didn't choose and couldn't have scheduled. Some Tuesday in March you'll be fed up with something, and that will do more than any list written on a hangover with a pen you had to search for.

So if you've already forgotten what you resolved this year, maybe don't feel bad. You didn't fail at a resolution. You just found out it was never really yours. The real one is coming. It just doesn't know the date yet.

# Why most New Year's resolutions fail (and the one of mine that didn't)

Every January most of us pick something and quit it by February. I don't think that's a character flaw. I think most resolutions are built in a way that makes quitting easy, and the fix is in the design, not the person.

Here's what usually goes wrong.

**1. The goal is a direction, not a thing you do.** "Get fit." "Read more." "Learn a language." You can't do "learn a language" on a Tuesday. Until the resolution becomes a specific action of a specific size, one lesson, one chapter, one walk, there's nothing to actually start, so you don't.

**2. It's sized for January-you.** On the first of the month you're rested and keen, so you plan for someone with an hour a day and no bad weeks. Then February happens. A resolution that only works when you're at your best won't survive the first ordinary week.

**3. Nobody would notice if you stopped.** This is the big one, and it's the one the Welsh thing taught me. Most resolutions are private. You tell no one, or you tell people once and they forget. So when you miss a day, the only person who knows is you, and you are very easy to talk round.

**4. There's no plan for the first slip.** The first missed day feels like the end because the plan never had a line for what happens after a miss. One day off becomes "well, that's over," and the whole thing folds.

## The one that stuck

I've been learning Welsh on an app for 700 days straight. I don't think that's because I'm unusually disciplined. It's because my 12-year-old does it too, and at dinner we check each other's streaks.

Look at that against the list. The action is small and specific: open the app, keep the streak alive. It fits a bad day. And the check isn't something I have to remember to do. It just happens, at a table I'm already sitting at, with someone who will absolutely notice if my number didn't go up. I don't have to supply the willpower. The setup supplies it.

So if you're picking a resolution this year, skip the dramatic one and ask three questions instead. What's the smallest version I'd do on a rough day? Who's going to see whether I did it? And when does that check happen, not "sometime," but a specific spot that's already in your week?

Get those three right and you don't need to be a better person in January. You just need a better setup.

You're tired, broke, back at work, and every routine you had got scrambled over the holidays. The one day everyone agrees to begin new habits is also one of the worst days of the year to begin anything.

**Count the attempts**

Every January someone writes that most New Year's resolutions fail. The numbers vary, the conclusion doesn't: people set goals, people quit, the gym empties out by February.

The frame is wrong. Most attempts fail. That's not the same thing, and the difference matters.

I smoked for fifteen years. I quit on my fourth serious attempt, and I've been clean for six. By the usual way of counting, the first three attempts were failures. Three resolutions, three collapses. That's the story the "most resolutions fail" articles would tell about me, right up until the fourth one happened to stick.

But that isn't what happened. Attempt two lasted five weeks and broke at a wedding. Counted as an outcome, that's five weeks of work gone over one evening. Counted as anything else, it was information. Weddings and drinking were my trigger. I didn't know that going in, and nothing short of standing at a wedding with a drink in my hand was going to tell me. By attempt four I knew, and attempt four was planned around exactly that.

The same goes for the rest. The first three attempts, between them, taught me where the cigarette actually lived: the first coffee, driving, and my brother. Not "stress", not "habit". Those three specific things. I didn't know those going in either. The attempts found them. Attempt four wasn't a better resolution. It was the same resolution with three attempts' worth of data behind it.

So here's the counting mistake. If you count outcomes, I failed three times and succeeded once. If you count attempts, I made four, each better informed than the last, and the fourth closed it out. Most people who quit smoking for good needed several tries. That isn't a sign their resolution was weak. It's how it normally goes.

This changes what a broken attempt means. It doesn't mean you lacked willpower, and it doesn't mean the resolution was wrong. It means you now know something you couldn't have learned any other way: the exact situation that gets you. Write it down. Next attempt, that situation is the thing you plan around.

Most resolutions don't fail. Most attempts do, and the resolution is what's left standing across them. If your January attempt breaks, look at where it broke. That's the whole point of it.

# Count the attempts

I quit smoking on my fourth serious attempt. I'd smoked for fifteen years. I'm six years clean now.

If you only look at the last attempt, that's a success story. If you look at the first three, it's three failures. Both readings are wrong, and the second one is the one that does the damage every January.

# The Skill We Can't Afford to Lose

*Five-minute all-hands talk*

## 1. The opening: AI is genuinely making us better (0:00–0:45)

**Opening paragraph:**

I want to start by saying something that might sound contradictory given the title of this talk: I think AI coding assistants are one of the best things to happen to engineering in years. I use them myself. They help us move faster, explore ideas we might otherwise not have had time to explore, and take care of work that doesn't necessarily require our deepest attention. And in a business like ours, where the systems we build determine whether trucks move, whether deliveries happen and whether customers can trust us, that kind of leverage matters. But I think there's a question we're not asking enough: as we get better at making machines do the work, are we getting worse at understanding the work ourselves?

## 2. What we're getting right, and what we might be losing (0:45–1:30)

Acknowledge the genuine benefits:

- Faster development and prototyping.
- Less time spent on repetitive coding.
- More room to focus on architecture and higher-value problems.
- Better leverage for engineers across the organisation.

Then introduce the distinction:

There is a difference between being able to produce code and being able to understand a system.

AI can help us produce code. But when something breaks at 2am, we need engineers who understand what they're looking at.

Our responsibility isn't just to ship features. It's to keep the business running.

## 3. The signal we're seeing (1:30–2:30)

Bring in the data:

Over the last six months, our median time-to-resolve for P2 incidents has increased from 38 minutes to 61 minutes.

That's a roughly 61% increase.

Be careful not to claim AI caused this. There could be multiple contributing factors. But it is a signal worth investigating.

Then share what you're seeing in incident reviews:

- Engineers struggling to read stack traces.
- Difficulty tracing an error through code they helped write.
- Less confidence in reasoning through a problem without immediately asking an assistant.

The important point:

This isn't about engineers being less capable. It's about the habits we're building as an organisation.

## 4. The 2am incident (2:30–3:30)

Tell the story without identifying the engineer.

One night, we had an outage. The on-call engineer was trying to resolve it and did what many of us would instinctively do: pasted the error into an AI assistant.

Four times.

Four different answers. Four confident suggested fixes.

Meanwhile, the actual problem was sitting in the logs. It took roughly ten minutes of reading through them to identify what was happening.

The lesson isn't that the engineer shouldn't have used AI. The lesson is that when the tool couldn't reliably diagnose the issue, we needed someone who could reason independently.

**The dangerous situation isn't an AI giving us a wrong answer. It's an engineer not knowing how to recognise that the answer is wrong.**

## 5. The aviation analogy (3:30–4:15)

Think about commercial aviation.

Modern aircraft have extraordinarily sophisticated autopilot systems. Pilots don't spend every flight manually controlling every aspect of the aircraft.

But pilots still train to fly manually.

Why?

Because automation handles the routine. Human skill matters when the routine breaks down.

You don't learn to hand-fly a plane because you expect to do it every day. You learn because when automation hands you a mess at the worst possible moment, you need to know how to fly.

Engineering is no different.

AI should be our autopilot, not our replacement for understanding how to fly.

## 6. The concrete ask (4:15–4:45)

Here's what I'd like us to consider:

For the first six months of a junior engineer's career, let them use AI to write code, explore solutions and accelerate development.

But ask them to debug without an AI assistant.

Let them read the logs, trace the stack, understand the failure and explain the root cause themselves before turning to an assistant.

Managers should support this as a deliberate training practice, not treat it as a productivity penalty.

This isn't about making people slower. It's about building the foundational skills that make them effective when things go wrong.

## 7. Closing (4:45–5:00)

I don't want us to become an organisation that is slower because it refuses to use AI.

I want us to become an organisation that can move faster because it knows when to use AI, when to question it, and when it needs a human who genuinely understands the system.

**Let's make sure we're building engineers who can use the autopilot, but can still fly the plane.**

## **1. Speech outline (5 minutes)**

**Working title: Are We Using AI to Build Better Software, or Just More Software?**

| Time      | Section            | What to cover                                                                                                                                                                        |
| --------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 0:00–0:45 | The anecdote       | Start with a relatable scenario: asking AI to write a piece of code, getting an answer in seconds, and feeling like you've accomplished something.                                   |
| 0:45–1:30 | The opportunity    | Acknowledge how incredible AI coding assistants are. Faster development, less repetitive work, quicker debugging, and more time for complex problems.                                |
| 1:30–2:30 | The catch          | Speed isn't the same as quality. AI can produce code that looks correct, compiles, and even passes basic tests while introducing edge cases, unnecessary complexity, or subtle bugs. |
| 2:30–3:30 | The responsibility | Engineers must understand, review, challenge, and test what AI generates. Don't outsource engineering judgement.                                                                     |
| 3:30–4:30 | The QA perspective | More code produced faster means we need to be equally thoughtful about validation. In insurance software, correctness and reliability matter enormously.                             |
| 4:30–5:00 | The conclusion     | Encourage everyone to use AI, experiment, and embrace it, but never confuse accepting an AI suggestion with engineering a solution.                                                  |

## **2. Opening paragraph**

I want to start with a situation I think most of us have experienced by now. You open Cursor, Claude, or whichever AI coding assistant you prefer, describe what you want to build, and within a few seconds, you have 100 lines of code sitting in front of you. It looks clean, it looks convincing, and for a moment, you feel incredibly productive. And honestly, you probably are. But here's something I've been thinking about: **just because AI can write code faster than we can, does that necessarily mean we're building better software?** I don't think the answer is always yes, and I think that's a conversation worth having.

## **3. Three key arguments to develop**

I'd keep coming back to these throughout the speech.

**Argument 1: AI is an accelerator, not a replacement for judgement.**

- Use it for boilerplate, repetitive tasks, debugging, documentation and exploring unfamiliar code.
- Let it save time on things that don't require your deepest thinking.
- But don't let it make decisions you don't understand.

**Argument 2: The speed-quality trade-off is real.**

- Code that compiles isn't necessarily good code.
- Code that passes a test isn't necessarily robust code.
- AI can introduce unnecessary abstractions, overlooked edge cases and subtle bugs.
- The faster we generate code, the more important thoughtful reviews become.

**Argument 3: Ownership doesn't transfer to AI.**

- If AI writes the code, the engineer still owns the outcome.
- You should be able to explain what the code does and why it works.
- You should be comfortable questioning or rejecting its suggestions.
- Particularly in insurance software, a small defect can have consequences beyond a failed feature.

## **4. The closing thought**

I'd finish with something conversational rather than overly motivational:

I don't think the solution is to use AI less. If anything, I think we should be experimenting with it more. The opportunity is enormous, and I don't think we should ignore it. But I do think we need to change how we measure productivity. It's not about how many lines of code we can generate, how quickly we can close a ticket, or how much work we can delegate to an AI assistant. It's about whether we're actually building better, more reliable software. So my take is simple: use AI, challenge it, learn from it, and let it make you faster. But never switch off your engineering judgement. Because at the end of the day, AI might write the code, but we're still responsible for what we ship.

# Count the attempts

I quit smoking on my fourth serious attempt. I'd smoked for fifteen years. I'm six years clean now.

If you only look at the last attempt, that's a success story. If you look at the first three, it's three failures. Both readings are wrong, and the second one is the one that does the damage every January.

"Most New Year's resolutions fail" is true, but it's measuring the wrong unit. It treats one attempt as the whole thing. Most attempts at anything hard fail. Ask anyone who has quit smoking for good how many times they quit before the one that stuck. The answer is almost never once.

So the question isn't why your resolution failed. It's what the attempt told you.

Attempt two lasted five weeks and died at a wedding. I could have filed that as "five weeks, failed," and for a while I did. What it actually said was: drinking at a wedding will take you out. Not drinking in general. Not weddings in general. The two together. Specific, repeatable, worth knowing.

Attempt four was planned around exactly that. Not around willpower, not around a date on a calendar. Around the thing I'd already watched break.

The first three attempts, between them, gave me the full list: first coffee of the morning, driving, and my brother. You don't find those by sitting and thinking about it. You find them by failing in front of them. Each attempt broke in a particular place, and the place was the information.

That's the reframe. Count attempts, not outcomes. A failed attempt isn't a mark against you, and it isn't a "lesson" in the vague sense either. It's a location. Where exactly did it go? What time of day, who was there, what was in your hand? Write that down and you have the plan for the next one.

This is not an argument that failure is secretly fine. It isn't. Three failed quits is three times I went back to something I'd said I was done with. But "failed" is only the verdict if you stop counting. If you're on attempt three, you're not someone who failed twice. You're someone two attempts in, holding two pieces of data most people never bother to collect.

The resolution frame wants you to grade the year. Don't. Note where it broke, and go again.

The same goes for the rest. The first three attempts, between them, taught me where the cigarette actually lived: the first coffee, driving, and my brother. Not "stress", not "habit". Those three specific things. I didn't know those going in either. The attempts found them. Attempt four wasn't a better resolution. It was the same resolution with three attempts' worth of data behind it.

So here's the counting mistake. If you count outcomes, I failed three times and succeeded once. If you count attempts, I made four, each better informed than the last, and the fourth closed it out. Most people who quit smoking for good needed several tries. That isn't a sign their resolution was weak. It's how it normally goes.

This changes what a broken attempt means. It doesn't mean you lacked willpower, and it doesn't mean the resolution was wrong. It means you now know something you couldn't have learned any other way: the exact situation that gets you. Write it down. Next attempt, that situation is the thing you plan around.

Most resolutions don't fail. Most attempts do, and the resolution is what's left standing across them. If your January attempt breaks, look at where it broke. That's the whole point of it.

# Why most New Year's resolutions fail (and the one of mine that didn't)

Every January most of us pick something and quit it by February. I don't think that's a character flaw. I think most resolutions are built in a way that makes quitting easy, and the fix is in the design, not the person.

Here's what usually goes wrong.

**1. The goal is a direction, not a thing you do.** "Get fit." "Read more." "Learn a language." You can't do "learn a language" on a Tuesday. Until the resolution becomes a specific action of a specific size, one lesson, one chapter, one walk, there's nothing to actually start, so you don't.

**2. It's sized for January-you.** On the first of the month you're rested and keen, so you plan for someone with an hour a day and no bad weeks. Then February happens. A resolution that only works when you're at your best won't survive the first ordinary week.

**3. Nobody would notice if you stopped.** This is the big one, and it's the one the Welsh thing taught me. Most resolutions are private. You tell no one, or you tell people once and they forget. So when you miss a day, the only person who knows is you, and you are very easy to talk round.

**4. There's no plan for the first slip.** The first missed day feels like the end because the plan never had a line for what happens after a miss. One day off becomes "well, that's over," and the whole thing folds.

## The one that stuck

I've been learning Welsh on an app for 700 days straight. I don't think that's because I'm unusually disciplined. It's because my 12-year-old does it too, and at dinner we check each other's streaks.

Look at that against the list. The action is small and specific: open the app, keep the streak alive. It fits a bad day. And the check isn't something I have to remember to do. It just happens, at a table I'm already sitting at, with someone who will absolutely notice if my number didn't go up. I don't have to supply the willpower. The setup supplies it.

So if you're picking a resolution this year, skip the dramatic one and ask three questions instead. What's the smallest version I'd do on a rough day? Who's going to see whether I did it? And when does that check happen, not "sometime," but a specific spot that's already in your week?

Get those three right and you don't need to be a better person in January. You just need a better setup.

**Why most New Year's resolutions fail**

I've got a 700-day streak on a Welsh app. My daughter, who is 12, is learning it too, and at dinner we check each other's streaks. It's become one of those small rituals a family picks up without deciding to. Somebody asks "did you do your Welsh?" and if the answer is no, you get up from the table and do it.

I've been thinking about why that one has held, because most things like it don't. The usual explanation for failed resolutions is that people aren't disciplined enough, or they pick the wrong goal, or they aim too high. I don't think it's any of those. I think it's simpler. People lose motivation. Everyone does. The feeling you had on January 1st isn't a character trait, it's a mood, and moods go. The question is what's left when it does.

For most resolutions, the honest answer is nothing. The goal was carried entirely by wanting it, and once the wanting fades, there's no reason to keep going that isn't "I said I would." That's a thin reason on a Tuesday night when you're tired. Nobody is watching, nobody will notice, and skipping costs you nothing you can feel.

What's different about the Welsh isn't that I want it more than other things I've wanted. It's that the habit stopped being mine alone. There's a person across the table who will ask. There's a number that goes back to zero if I don't. And there's a fixed point in the day, dinner, where it comes up whether I'm in the mood or not. None of that requires motivation. On the days I have some, fine. On the days I don't, the structure does the job instead.

I'd put it this way: a resolution is a promise to yourself, and promises to yourself are the easiest kind to break, because you're the only one who has to agree to let it go. The habits that stick are the ones you've handed partly to someone else, or to a routine that runs without you having to feel anything about it.

So if you're making one this year, I wouldn't spend much time on the goal. Spend it on what will keep the goal alive in March, when you've gone off it. Who's going to ask you about it? When, in the day, does it come up on its own? If you can't answer those, you're relying on a feeling to last, and feelings don't.

# Why resolutions fail: the date was always the problem

I've made New Year's resolutions. I couldn't tell you what any of them were. None of them failed dramatically. I didn't cave in week three and eat a cake with my hands. I just forgot I'd made them, which is somehow worse. You can't even learn from a goal you can't remember.

I think that's how most resolutions actually go, and I think the date is to blame. Not willpower. Not vagueness. January 1st.

**1. Nothing in your life changed on January 1st**

A real reason to change usually comes from something: a comment from a doctor, a bill, a photo, a week that went badly. Resolutions come from a calendar. The year rolled over, so a goal was supposed to follow. But a goal that arrives on schedule has no event holding it in place. It's a promise made because it was the time for promises, which is exactly why it slides off.

**2. You picked it from the menu**

When the date is the prompt, you reach for the stock answers: eat better, move more, read more. Not because those are your problems, but because they're the kind of thing people resolve. A goal chosen from a list was never personal, and nothing impersonal survives a dull Tuesday.

**3. It's a terrible week to start anything**

You're tired, broke, back at work, and every routine you had got scrambled over the holidays. The one day everyone agrees to begin new habits is also one of the worst days of the year to begin anything.

**4. It's annual, so it just expires**

If you set goals once a year, the one that slips has to wait twelve months. Nobody re-sets a resolution in March. It doesn't fail. It quietly reaches the end of its shelf life.

**What to do instead**

- Pick the thing that's actually bugging you, even if it's boring and nobody else would resolve it.
- Choose an unremarkable start date: a normal Tuesday in a normal week.
- Write it down somewhere you'll see it. Worst case, next January you'll at least know what you forgot.

## The Problem With January 1st

I've made a few New Year's resolutions. I can't tell you what most of them were. That's not a confession, it's the whole point.

The usual explanation for why resolutions fail is that they're badly built. Too vague, too big, no plan. Set smaller goals, track them, stack them onto habits you already have. All true, probably. But it skips over something stranger: why are we all trying to change on the same day?

Every other decision to change comes from somewhere. You start running because your knees ache going up the stairs. You quit something because you catch your reflection and don't like it. You save money because the account hit a number that scared you. The change has a cause, and the cause arrived first.

New Year's Day reverses that. The date shows up and demands a reason. So you go looking for one, and you find something plausible: read more, drink less, call people back. It sounds like a goal. It's really just an answer to the question "well, what are you going to do?"

Nothing in your life has shifted between December 31st and January 1st. Your schedule is the same. The things that made the old habit easy are all still there. The only thing that's different is the calendar, and the calendar has never once stopped anyone from doing anything.

This is why forgetting them is so easy. There's nothing to remember them by. A change you made because of a real moment has that moment attached to it — you can go back to it when you waver. A change you made because it was January has January attached to it, and by the third week that's gone.

I don't think the fix is better resolutions. I think it's noticing that the ones that stick tend to start on unremarkable days, for reasons you didn't choose and couldn't have scheduled. Some Tuesday in March you'll be fed up with something, and that will do more than any list written on a hangover with a pen you had to search for.

So if you've already forgotten what you resolved this year, maybe don't feel bad. You didn't fail at a resolution. You just found out it was never really yours. The real one is coming. It just doesn't know the date yet.

# Count the attempts

I quit smoking on my fourth serious attempt. I'd smoked for fifteen years. I'm six years clean now.

If you only look at the last attempt, that's a success story. If you look at the first three, it's three failures. Both readings are wrong, and the second one is the one that does the damage every January.

"Most New Year's resolutions fail" is true, but it's measuring the wrong unit. It treats one attempt as the whole thing. Most attempts at anything hard fail. Ask anyone who has quit smoking for good how many times they quit before the one that stuck. The answer is almost never once.

So the question isn't why your resolution failed. It's what the attempt told you.

Attempt two lasted five weeks and died at a wedding. I could have filed that as "five weeks, failed," and for a while I did. What it actually said was: drinking at a wedding will take you out. Not drinking in general. Not weddings in general. The two together. Specific, repeatable, worth knowing.

Attempt four was planned around exactly that. Not around willpower, not around a date on a calendar. Around the thing I'd already watched break.

The first three attempts, between them, gave me the full list: first coffee of the morning, driving, and my brother. You don't find those by sitting and thinking about it. You find them by failing in front of them. Each attempt broke in a particular place, and the place was the information.

That's the reframe. Count attempts, not outcomes. A failed attempt isn't a mark against you, and it isn't a "lesson" in the vague sense either. It's a location. Where exactly did it go? What time of day, who was there, what was in your hand? Write that down and you have the plan for the next one.

This is not an argument that failure is secretly fine. It isn't. Three failed quits is three times I went back to something I'd said I was done with. But "failed" is only the verdict if you stop counting. If you're on attempt three, you're not someone who failed twice. You're someone two attempts in, holding two pieces of data most people never bother to collect.

The resolution frame wants you to grade the year. Don't. Note where it broke, and go again.

# Maybe You Haven't Failed Yet

Every January, millions of people make resolutions. By February, a good number have abandoned them. We call these failed resolutions, talk about a lack of discipline, blame unrealistic expectations, and move on to the next year.

I think we're looking at it all wrong.

We have an odd habit of judging an attempt by its outcome. If you set out to change something and don't manage it, you've failed. But why? Since when did the first attempt have to be the successful one?

I quit smoking on my fourth serious attempt. Six years later, I haven't touched a cigarette.

My first three attempts weren't particularly successful if you measure success by the number of days I stayed away from cigarettes. But each one taught me something.

The second attempt lasted five weeks. I eventually gave in at a wedding. That taught me something important: weddings, drinking and the social environment around them were triggers I hadn't accounted for.

Other attempts revealed different patterns. The first coffee of the morning. Driving. Even spending time with my brother.

By the fourth attempt, I wasn't simply telling myself I was going to quit. I knew what I was up against. I had identified the situations that made it difficult and planned around them.

Six years on, I find it difficult to call those first three attempts failures. Without them, I might never have made the fourth one work.

And this isn't particularly unusual. Research on smoking cessation has consistently found that many successful quitters make several attempts before stopping for good. The journey isn't always a straight line from decision to achievement.

Yet every January, we approach resolutions as though they come with a pass-or-fail deadline.

Perhaps we should stop doing that.

If you decide to exercise regularly and give up after three weeks, that's an attempt. If you try to save money and find yourself back where you started by March, that's an attempt too. The useful question isn't simply why you failed. It's what you discovered that you didn't know before.

What got in the way? What situation caught you off guard? What would you do differently next time?

I'm not suggesting that trying is the same as achieving. It isn't. But treating every unsuccessful attempt as a failure is a pretty good way of ensuring you never learn from it.

So, if your New Year's resolution didn't survive the year, don't just cross it off the list.

Look at what happened. There might be something in there worth taking into your next attempt.

You may not be starting again. You may simply be starting with better information.

**The resolution advice was never written for you**

Every piece of advice about keeping a resolution assumes you have a morning. Not a morning as in the thing that happens after you sleep. A morning as in 6am, same wall clock, Monday to Friday, followed by a commute and a desk. "Same time every day." "Build a morning routine." "Do it before work so nothing gets in the way."

If you work rotating 12s, or a warehouse floor, or you're up with a newborn, none of that is a plan. It's a description of someone else's week.

Here's mine. Three years in a row I resolved to be a 6am gym person. Three years in a row it was dead by February, and not for any of the reasons the articles list. My rotation would flip to nights, and 6am stopped being a time I could do anything with. On nights, 6am is either the middle of your sleep or the tail end of a shift. The habit wasn't failing. The clock it was tied to had stopped meaning anything.

That's the part the resolution articles get wrong. They look at the February drop-off and decide the person was vague, or overambitious, or didn't want it badly enough. Nobody checks whether the advice fit the life it was handed to. If your schedule doesn't repeat, "same time every day" isn't a rule you failed to keep. It's a rule with nowhere to attach.

What finally worked for me wasn't a better alarm. It was swapping the clock for an event. The gym is the first thing I do after any shift ends. Day shift, night shift, doesn't matter. Shift ends, I go. That's held for 14 months now, across every rotation flip, which is roughly a year longer than any of the 6am versions managed.

The difference is that a shift ending happens in every version of my week. 6am doesn't. The anchor has to be something your life reliably produces, not something a calendar produces.

Maybe it's the baby going down, whenever that turns out to be. Hang the habit on that. If the thing you pick disappears when your rotation changes, it was never going to hold, and that's not a verdict on you.

The advice isn't bad. It's just addressed to someone with a 9-to-5. Feel free to forward it along.

# Why Most New Year's Resolutions Fail (And Maybe It's Not Your Fault)

Every January, we do the same thing. We convince ourselves that this is the year we'll finally get our lives together. We set goals, buy gym memberships, download habit trackers, and promise ourselves that we'll wake up at 5 or 6 AM every morning.

There's just one problem with that advice: it assumes we all live the same life.

Three years in a row, I made the same New Year's resolution. Get to the gym at 6 AM. Three years in a row, I had given up by February.

For a while, I blamed myself. Maybe I wasn't disciplined enough. Maybe I lacked consistency. Maybe I just didn't want it badly enough.

Then I looked at my schedule.

I'm an ER nurse. I rotate between 12-hour day and night shifts every few weeks. A 6 AM gym session sounds great until you've just finished a night shift, haven't slept properly, and your body has absolutely no interest in cooperating.

And that's when it hit me: maybe the problem wasn't my willpower. Maybe the advice was never designed for someone like me.

Most habit-building advice seems to come from the perspective of someone with a predictable 9-to-5 job. Wake up at the same time. Exercise every morning. Follow a routine. Build consistency.

Great advice, if your schedule allows it.

But what about nurses? Warehouse workers? Parents with newborns? Anyone whose working hours, responsibilities, or sleep patterns change constantly?

We keep treating the inability to follow a fixed routine as a personal failure, when the routine itself might be completely unrealistic.

What finally worked for me was changing one thing: I stopped attaching my gym habit to a time and started attaching it to an event.

The gym became the first thing I do after every shift, whether that's a day shift or a night shift. No 6 AM target. No rigid timetable. Just one consistent trigger.

I've kept that going for 14 months now. Something I couldn't sustain for three consecutive Februaries has become part of my life.

So, if your New Year's resolutions keep falling apart, maybe stop asking yourself why you lack discipline. Start asking whether the system you're trying to follow actually fits your life.

Find an anchor that works with your schedule, not against it. It could be after a shift, after dropping the kids off, or before heading home.

Your routine doesn't have to look like everyone else's to work.

And honestly, that's probably the point.

**The resolution advice was never written for you**

Every piece of advice about keeping a resolution assumes you have a morning. Not a morning as in the thing that happens after you sleep. A morning as in 6am, same wall clock, Monday to Friday, followed by a commute and a desk. "Same time every day." "Build a morning routine." "Do it before work so nothing gets in the way."

If you work rotating 12s, or a warehouse floor, or you're up with a newborn, none of that is a plan. It's a description of someone else's week.

Here's mine. Three years in a row I resolved to be a 6am gym person. Three years in a row it was dead by February, and not for any of the reasons the articles list. My rotation would flip to nights, and 6am stopped being a time I could do anything with. On nights, 6am is either the middle of your sleep or the tail end of a shift. The habit wasn't failing. The clock it was tied to had stopped meaning anything.

That's the part the resolution articles get wrong. They look at the February drop-off and decide the person was vague, or overambitious, or didn't want it badly enough. Nobody checks whether the advice fit the life it was handed to. If your schedule doesn't repeat, "same time every day" isn't a rule you failed to keep. It's a rule with nowhere to attach.

What finally worked for me wasn't a better alarm. It was swapping the clock for an event. The gym is the first thing I do after any shift ends. Day shift, night shift, doesn't matter. Shift ends, I go. That's held for 14 months now, across every rotation flip, which is roughly a year longer than any of the 6am versions managed.

The difference is that a shift ending happens in every version of my week. 6am doesn't. The anchor has to be something your life reliably produces, not something a calendar produces.

So if you're planning something for January: before you write down a time, ask what in your week actually repeats. Maybe it's clocking out. Maybe it's handover. Maybe it's the baby going down, whenever that turns out to be. Hang the habit on that. If the thing you pick disappears when your rotation changes, it was never going to hold, and that's not a verdict on you.

The advice isn't bad. It's just addressed to someone with a 9-to-5. Feel free to forward it along.

# Maybe You Haven't Failed Yet

Every January, millions of people make resolutions. By February, a good number have abandoned them. We call these failed resolutions, talk about a lack of discipline, blame unrealistic expectations, and move on to the next year.

I think we're looking at it all wrong.

We have an odd habit of judging an attempt by its outcome. If you set out to change something and don't manage it, you've failed. But why? Since when did the first attempt have to be the successful one?

I quit smoking on my fourth serious attempt. Six years later, I haven't touched a cigarette.

My first three attempts weren't particularly successful if you measure success by the number of days I stayed away from cigarettes. But each one taught me something.

The second attempt lasted five weeks. I eventually gave in at a wedding. That taught me something important: weddings, drinking and the social environment around them were triggers I hadn't accounted for.

Other attempts revealed different patterns. The first coffee of the morning. Driving. Even spending time with my brother.

By the fourth attempt, I wasn't simply telling myself I was going to quit. I knew what I was up against. I had identified the situations that made it difficult and planned around them.

Six years on, I find it difficult to call those first three attempts failures. Without them, I might never have made the fourth one work.

And this isn't particularly unusual. Research on smoking cessation has consistently found that many successful quitters make several attempts before stopping for good. The journey isn't always a straight line from decision to achievement.

Yet every January, we approach resolutions as though they come with a pass-or-fail deadline.

Perhaps we should stop doing that.

If you decide to exercise regularly and give up after three weeks, that's an attempt. If you try to save money and find yourself back where you started by March, that's an attempt too. The useful question isn't simply why you failed. It's what you discovered that you didn't know before.

What got in the way? What situation caught you off guard? What would you do differently next time?

I'm not suggesting that trying is the same as achieving. It isn't. But treating every unsuccessful attempt as a failure is a pretty good way of ensuring you never learn from it.

So, if your New Year's resolution didn't survive the year, don't just cross it off the list.

Look at what happened. There might be something in there worth taking into your next attempt.

You may not be starting again. You may simply be starting with better information.

# Count the attempts

I quit smoking on my fourth serious attempt. I'd smoked for fifteen years. I'm six years clean now.

If you only look at the last attempt, that's a success story. If you look at the first three, it's three failures. Both readings are wrong, and the second one is the one that does the damage every January.

"Most New Year's resolutions fail" is true, but it's measuring the wrong unit. It treats one attempt as the whole thing. Most attempts at anything hard fail. Ask anyone who has quit smoking for good how many times they quit before the one that stuck. The answer is almost never once.

So the question isn't why your resolution failed. It's what the attempt told you.

Attempt two lasted five weeks and died at a wedding. I could have filed that as "five weeks, failed," and for a while I did. What it actually said was: drinking at a wedding will take you out. Not drinking in general. Not weddings in general. The two together. Specific, repeatable, worth knowing.

Attempt four was planned around exactly that. Not around willpower, not around a date on a calendar. Around the thing I'd already watched break.

The first three attempts, between them, gave me the full list: first coffee of the morning, driving, and my brother. You don't find those by sitting and thinking about it. You find them by failing in front of them. Each attempt broke in a particular place, and the place was the information.

That's the reframe. Count attempts, not outcomes. A failed attempt isn't a mark against you, and it isn't a "lesson" in the vague sense either. It's a location. Where exactly did it go? What time of day, who was there, what was in your hand? Write that down and you have the plan for the next one.

This is not an argument that failure is secretly fine. It isn't. Three failed quits is three times I went back to something I'd said I was done with. But "failed" is only the verdict if you stop counting. If you're on attempt three, you're not someone who failed twice. You're someone two attempts in, holding two pieces of data most people never bother to collect.

The resolution frame wants you to grade the year. Don't. Note where it broke, and go again.

**Why most New Year's resolutions fail**

I've got a 700-day streak on a Welsh app. My daughter, who is 12, is learning it too, and at dinner we check each other's streaks. It's become one of those small rituals a family picks up without deciding to. Somebody asks "did you do your Welsh?" and if the answer is no, you get up from the table and do it.

I've been thinking about why that one has held, because most things like it don't. The usual explanation for failed resolutions is that people aren't disciplined enough, or they pick the wrong goal, or they aim too high. I don't think it's any of those. I think it's simpler. People lose motivation. Everyone does. The feeling you had on January 1st isn't a character trait, it's a mood, and moods go. The question is what's left when it does.

For most resolutions, the honest answer is nothing. The goal was carried entirely by wanting it, and once the wanting fades, there's no reason to keep going that isn't "I said I would." That's a thin reason on a Tuesday night when you're tired. Nobody is watching, nobody will notice, and skipping costs you nothing you can feel.

What's different about the Welsh isn't that I want it more than other things I've wanted. It's that the habit stopped being mine alone. There's a person across the table who will ask. There's a number that goes back to zero if I don't. And there's a fixed point in the day, dinner, where it comes up whether I'm in the mood or not. None of that requires motivation. On the days I have some, fine. On the days I don't, the structure does the job instead.

I'd put it this way: a resolution is a promise to yourself, and promises to yourself are the easiest kind to break, because you're the only one who has to agree to let it go. The habits that stick are the ones you've handed partly to someone else, or to a routine that runs without you having to feel anything about it.

So if you're making one this year, I wouldn't spend much time on the goal. Spend it on what will keep the goal alive in March, when you've gone off it. Who's going to ask you about it? When, in the day, does it come up on its own? If you can't answer those, you're relying on a feeling to last, and feelings don't.

# Why Most New Year's Resolutions Fail

Every year, as December comes to an end, we find ourselves making promises to a future version of ourselves. We'll go to the gym, read more books, spend less time on our phones, eat healthier, or finally learn that skill we've been putting off. For a few days, sometimes even a few weeks, we're genuinely committed. And then, slowly, things go back to normal.

So, why does this happen?

I think the biggest reason most New Year's resolutions fail is that we rely too heavily on motivation.

There's something about the beginning of a new year that makes change feel exciting. A fresh calendar, a clean slate, and the feeling that this time things will be different. Motivation is at an all-time high, and suddenly, waking up at 5 AM or going for a run every morning doesn't seem so difficult.

But motivation is an emotion, and like most emotions, it comes and goes.

Eventually, the excitement wears off. You have a long day, it's raining outside, you don't feel like going to the gym, or you simply have other things on your mind. And that's when the real test begins. Unfortunately, most resolutions aren't built to survive those moments.

We often mistake wanting something badly for being prepared to work towards it consistently. The two are very different.

The problem isn't necessarily that we set ambitious goals. It's that we build our plans around the assumption that we'll feel motivated every single day. We forget that progress is rarely exciting. More often than not, it's repetitive, inconvenient, and sometimes downright boring.

I think the solution is to stop treating resolutions as temporary bursts of enthusiasm and start treating them as habits.

Instead of promising to read 30 books in a year, start by reading five pages every day. Instead of committing to an intense workout routine, start with something you can realistically maintain. Make the barrier to starting as small as possible.

And perhaps most importantly, learn to show up even when you don't feel like it.

Missing a day shouldn't mean abandoning the entire goal. One bad week shouldn't become an excuse to give up for the rest of the year.

Ultimately, I don't think the people who achieve their New Year's resolutions are necessarily more motivated than everyone else. They're simply better at continuing when motivation disappears.

Maybe that's what we should focus on this January: not becoming a completely different person overnight, but becoming someone who keeps showing up, even on ordinary days.
